projects.name: UP-Dream
projects.tagline: A place for community, reflection, and the next small step.
projects.description: A member app for a church community, bringing attendance, announcements, schedules, reservations, personal reflection, and Bible reading into one place. I built the mobile experience and its shared backend, alongside a separate administrator app.

screens.title: Reflection, made visible
screens.alt: UP-Dream monthly gratitude and Bible-reflection records with synthetic demo data
screens.body: Review gratitude and Bible-reflection (QT) entries by date and return to the relevant recording flow.

screens.title: A considered reading experience
screens.alt: UP-Dream Bible entry with chapter navigation, bookmarks, and copyright information
screens.body: Choose a book and chapter, return to bookmarks, and read the copyright and permission notice.

projects.flowNote: Member and administrator clients share the backend. Database records and licensed Bible text have separate storage and access boundaries.

decisions.title: Recover a session without losing trust
decisions.body: Startup distinguishes temporary connection failures from invalid credentials. Refreshes can retain the last useful screen, while account or permission changes discard old data and invalidate delayed responses.

decisions.title: Make concurrent attendance edits explicit
decisions.body: Attendance writes use an expected version to detect conflicting edits. The server rechecks authority after acquiring a workflow lock, and commits the record, revision, and audit history together.

decisions.title: Refresh through the permission boundary
decisions.body: Realtime messages signal that something changed. Clients fetch the actual records again through the API so current permissions apply. Coalescing and short jitter windows limit redundant requests.

ai: I used Claude Code and Codex for scoped frontend work and integration. In the general-member faith-garden update, Claude Code prepared the initial growth and mission-screen changes; Codex handled the home screen, shared theme, calendar and reading-flow refinements, and integration checks.

ImageGen supplied static garden and mission-letter illustrations. Text, buttons, record indicators, and interactions remain native React Native elements. The screenshots here show the earlier interface for young-adult members. I define the product requirements and release scope.
rights: I handled the copyright review and the work to secure permission for the Korean 개역개정 translation used in UP-Dream. The project checklist records permission confirmation. Copyright remains with the Korean Bible Society, and the supporting documents are retained privately.

The reader provides all 66 books to approved members. The full text stays outside the app bundle and public repository, is delivered from private AWS S3 through an authenticated API, and is checked for integrity. The app displays copyright notices and uses an account-specific temporary cache that is cleared on logout and account changes.
projects.evidence: The technical overview documents source boundaries, design trade-offs, and dated test results, including session recovery, cache isolation, and concurrent writes.

projects.name: UP-Dream Admin
projects.tagline: The right tools for the people looking after a community.
projects.description: A native iPhone and iPad app for membership approvals, attendance, and daily operations. I brought the service’s administrative workflows to SwiftUI, with a separate administrator session and server-controlled capabilities.

screens.title: Daily operations on iPhone
screens.alt: UP-Dream Admin iPhone overview with synthetic approval and attendance counts
screens.body: Outstanding approvals, attendance summaries, and shortcuts provide entry points into daily work. All displayed figures are test fixtures.

screens.title: A larger view on iPad
screens.alt: UP-Dream Admin iPad operations overview with synthetic test data
screens.body: The same operational information uses the larger display. Counts illustrate the interface and are not service usage metrics.

projects.flowNote: The interface reflects server-provided capabilities. The API checks authorization again when reading or changing records.

decisions.title: Keep administrator sessions separate
decisions.body: Device-only Keychain storage and an ephemeral URLSession reduce retained session data. Relaunching the app requires fresh authorized reads instead of restoring a persistent offline management cache.

decisions.title: Reject responses from a previous session
decisions.body: Requests capture a session generation. A delayed response is discarded when it belongs to an earlier session or permission scope.

decisions.title: Preserve the meaning of attendance data
decisions.body: Unmarked records remain distinct from absences. Attendance analysis requires enough observation history before classifying a change, while conflicting edits have an explicit outcome.

ai: I used AI assistance for the SwiftUI frontend, including screen implementation and presentation. I defined the operational workflows and interface requirements.
projects.evidence: The technical overview connects native session handling, API authorization, and attendance behavior to selected XCTest and policy checks. It distinguishes executed checks from source review.

projects.name: Naerim · 내림
projects.tagline: Remember what made this cup worth making again.
projects.description: A native coffee journal for recording brews, keeping recipes, and comparing the conditions behind each cup. I built and released the app for iPhone and iPad, with Korean, English, and Japanese localization.

screens.title: Prepare another cup
screens.alt: Naerim preparation with sample beans, recipe, grinder setting, dose, water, and temperature
screens.body: Reuse earlier settings and change the variables that matter for this cup. Optional measurements stay separate from zero values.

screens.title: Follow the brewing plan
screens.alt: Naerim active brew timer, current pour target, and planned water graph
screens.body: Keep elapsed time, the current pour target, and the planned water sequence together during brewing.

screens.title: Learn from the last cup
screens.alt: Naerim searchable brew history with sample conditions, ratings, and equipment
screens.body: Search previous brews and inspect the conditions and ratings recorded for each one.

projects.flowNote: The interface edits value types. Repositories own persistence, while a shared coordinator manages an active or unsaved brew across app windows.

decisions.title: Keep the past independent of the catalog
decisions.body: A brew captures its recipe and equipment values as a historical snapshot. Editing or deleting catalog entries does not redefine the conditions of an earlier cup.

decisions.title: Recover unfinished work
decisions.body: A monotonic clock tracks elapsed time and atomic JSON checkpoints support relaunch recovery. Saving a result and removing its checkpoint are reconciled so a retry can recognize an already stored brew.

decisions.title: Validate before replacing the draft
decisions.body: Recipe scaling checks overflow, non-finite values, and rounding residuals before producing a replacement. A failed adjustment preserves the original draft. This case is available as a standalone Swift package.

ai: I used Codex for bounded development tasks. For the brew-entry refinement, I requested a simpler flow based on individually selected measurements. The implementation preserved missing values, target versus actual water amounts, and the separation between new drafts and previous results.

I define product behavior, choose which changes to accept, and own release decisions. Builds, XCTest results, UI checks, and source snapshots document what was verified. Brewing and comparison use native Swift data and calculation logic.
projects.evidence: The public recipe-validation package has 14 passing tests, including 324 deterministic ratio-and-target combinations, and a successful GitHub Actions run. The full app’s separate, dated verification is documented in its technical overview.
